Cubic collisions and uniform amplitudes

Two real critical points can merge and disappear. Expanding separately at each point then introduces coefficients that become singular at the merger. A smooth cubic coordinate instead gives two Airy profiles, with smooth amplitude coefficients on both sides of the collision. The same construction applies when one direction of a higher-dimensional Hessian degenerates and the remaining directions stay nondegenerate.

Throughout, phases are real and smooth, amplitudes may be complex, and . Parameter estimates refer to compact subsets of a specified small parameter neighborhood. All supports in the integration variables lie in fixed compact subsets of their coordinate domains. A zero-dimensional integral is evaluation.

Earlier proofs and the density convention

  • Classical finite-order preparation and division, S1–S42, F1–F42 and P1–P43, proves smooth division by a generic polynomial and by an original smooth divisor, including reality and linearity in the dividend. The remainder is polynomial in the original distinguished variable.
  • Smooth parameter flows, NF1–NF15, and flow inverses and continuation, NF16–NF21, prove the local solutions, all parameter derivatives, continuation and inverse maps used below.
  • Regular level sets and transverse convolution, Lemmas 0.1–0.2, proves real inverse and implicit maps. Zero hypersurfaces as curvature measures, Lemma 3.0, proves nonlinear substitution.
  • Finite-order phases and missing powers, Theorems 3 and 5 and Proposition 6, proves the scalar normalization, the entire Airy function and its two canonical integrals. Polynomial phases and Fourier tails, Theorem B and Solution 8, proves their Gaussian regularization with every frequency derivative.
  • Smooth quadratic coordinates, M1–M2 and P4–P5, proves the parameter Morse lemma and its Jacobian. Finite stationary jets and quadratic exchange, Theorem 1, proves the exact quadratic expansion and its differentiated-amplitude remainder.
  • The scalar, §§12–13, integration, §§15–16, and finite algebra, §10, foundations supply the derivative, compactness, partition, integration and matrix rules.

Changing an integration coordinate always changes the amplitude by the absolute Jacobian. In particular, a decreasing scalar coordinate contributes a positive density factor.

Proof. At each , the distinguished -order of is . Apply the earlier original-divisor division theorem with auxiliary parameters . Fix one actual common dividend neighborhood and one cutoff in for this application. Its quotient and remainder depend linearly on the dividend. They are real for real data and smooth in all the auxiliary parameters.

The polynomial remainder here follows from P40–P43: divide the cutoff dividend by the prepared monic polynomial, and divide its quotient by the nonvanishing unit. Multiplying a polynomial remainder by that unit is not this division.

Finitely many parameter neighborhoods cover . Shrink the neighborhoods to common neighborhoods contained in every selected product and choose a smooth partition in , with each factor compactly supported inside its selected -interval. Multiply each local identity by its factor and add. The factors sum to one on a neighborhood of ; extension by zero is smooth because their supports lie inside their intervals. This proves (C2) on the common product. For the cutoff dividend is the zero function, for every . Linearity makes every local output zero there, and hence makes the sum zero.
